claim: Dysfunctional and leaky blood vessels resulting from disruption of the endothelial cell (EC) barrier accompanies numerous diseases.
source: Dysfunctional and leaky blood vessels resulting from disruption of the endothelial cell (EC) barrier accompanies numerous diseases.
evidence: This is a general statement about disease pathology supported by the broader scientific literature context.

claim: The EC barrier is established through endothelial cell tight and adherens junctions.
source: The EC barrier is established through endothelial cell tight and adherens junctions.
evidence: This is established knowledge about EC barrier structure.

claim: Claudin5 exhibited diminishing expression along the arteriovenous axis across tissues.
source: Across tissues, Claudin5 exhibited diminishing expression along the arteriovenous axis, correlating with EC barrier integrity.
evidence: Supported by scRNAseq data analysis shown in Figure 1.

claim: Claudin5 expression correlates with EC barrier integrity.
source: Across tissues, Claudin5 exhibited diminishing expression along the arteriovenous axis, correlating with EC barrier integrity.
evidence: Supported by functional analysis and expression data.

claim: Functional analysis identified tissue-specific differences in leakage properties.
source: Functional analysis identified tissue-specific differences in leakage properties and response to the leakage agonist histamine.
evidence: Supported by permeability assays in different tissues shown in Figure 2.

claim: Functional analysis identified tissue-specific differences in response to the leakage agonist histamine.
source: Functional analysis identified tissue-specific differences in leakage properties and response to the leakage agonist histamine.
evidence: Supported by histamine-induced leakage experiments in Figure 2.

claim: Loss of Claudin5 enhanced histamine-induced leakage in an organotypic and vessel type-specific manner.
source: Loss of Claudin5 enhanced histamine-induced leakage in an organotypic and vessel type-specific manner in an inducible, EC-specific, knock-out mouse.
evidence: Supported by experiments using Cldn5 iECKO mice shown in Figures 3 and 4.

claim: Claudin5 loss left junction ultrastructure unaffected.
source: Mechanistically, Claudin5 loss left junction ultrastructure unaffected but altered its composition, with concomitant loss of zonula occludens-1 and upregulation of VE-Cadherin expression.
evidence: Supported by TEM analysis shown in Figure 5A-C.

claim: Claudin5 loss altered junction composition with concomitant loss of zonula occludens-1.
source: Mechanistically, Claudin5 loss left junction ultrastructure unaffected but altered its composition, with concomitant loss of zonula occludens-1 and upregulation of VE-Cadherin expression.
evidence: Supported by Western blot and immunohistochemistry data in Figure 5.

claim: Claudin5 loss resulted in upregulation of VE-Cadherin expression.
source: Mechanistically, Claudin5 loss left junction ultrastructure unaffected but altered its composition, with concomitant loss of zonula occludens-1 and upregulation of VE-Cadherin expression.
evidence: Supported by Western blot and immunohistochemistry data in Figure 5.

claim: Blood vessel dysfunction is a hallmark and contributing factor to the progression of numerous pathologies including solid tumours, ischemic diseases and inflammatory conditions.
source: Blood vessel dysfunction is a hallmark and contributing factor to the progression of numerous pathologies including solid tumours, ischemic diseases and inflammatory conditions (Lee et al., 2007; Burke and Miles, 1958; Hashizume et al., 2000).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: In pathologies, local concentrations of inflammatory cytokines and growth factors are increased, leading to weakening of the endothelial cell (EC) barrier.
source: In such pathologies, local concentrations of inflammatory cytokines and growth factors are increased, leading to weakening of the endothelial cell (EC) barrier, a regulatable interface between circulating blood and the surrounding tissue environment (Senger et al., 1983; Miles and Miles, 1952; Palade et al., 1979).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Loss of EC barrier integrity leads to enhanced molecular and cellular passage across the endothelium resulting in edema, tissue damage, atrophy, and disease progression.
source: Loss of EC barrier integrity in-turn leads to enhanced molecular and cellular passage across the endothelium resulting in edema, tissue damage, atrophy, and disease progression (Wu et al., 2014; Fleckenstein et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: EC barrier integrity is mediated primarily by adherens junctions (AJs) and tight junctions (TJs).
source: EC barrier integrity is mediated primarily by adherens junctions (AJs) and tight junctions (TJs), composed of transmembrane proteins forming intercellular interactions that bridge adjacent EC membranes (Corada et al., 1999; Claesson-Welsh et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: AJs and TJs are composed of transmembrane proteins forming intercellular interactions that bridge adjacent EC membranes.
source: EC barrier integrity is mediated primarily by adherens junctions (AJs) and tight junctions (TJs), composed of transmembrane proteins forming intercellular interactions that bridge adjacent EC membranes (Corada et al., 1999; Claesson-Welsh et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: AJs are ubiquitously distributed throughout the vascular system in all vessel subtypes (arterial, capillary, and venous).
source: AJs are ubiquitously distributed throughout the vascular system in all vessel subtypes (arterial, capillary, and venous) and consist of the largely endothelial-specific transmembrane protein vascular endothelial (VE)-Cadherin, which forms homophilic interactions between cells and associates intracellularly with the actin cytoskeleton via several members of the catenin family (Bazzoni and Dejana, 2004).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: AJs consist of the largely endothelial-specific transmembrane protein vascular endothelial (VE)-Cadherin.
source: AJs are ubiquitously distributed throughout the vascular system in all vessel subtypes (arterial, capillary, and venous) and consist of the largely endothelial-specific transmembrane protein vascular endothelial (VE)-Cadherin, which forms homophilic interactions between cells and associates intracellularly with the actin cytoskeleton via several members of the catenin family (Bazzoni and Dejana, 2004).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: VE-Cadherin forms homophilic interactions between cells.
source: AJs are ubiquitously distributed throughout the vascular system in all vessel subtypes (arterial, capillary, and venous) and consist of the largely endothelial-specific transmembrane protein vascular endothelial (VE)-Cadherin, which forms homophilic interactions between cells and associates intracellularly with the actin cytoskeleton via several members of the catenin family (Bazzoni and Dejana, 2004).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: VE-Cadherin associates intracellularly with the actin cytoskeleton via several members of the catenin family.
source: AJs are ubiquitously distributed throughout the vascular system in all vessel subtypes (arterial, capillary, and venous) and consist of the largely endothelial-specific transmembrane protein vascular endothelial (VE)-Cadherin, which forms homophilic interactions between cells and associates intracellularly with the actin cytoskeleton via several members of the catenin family (Bazzoni and Dejana, 2004).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: VE-cadherin-catenin interactions are highly regulated by their phosphorylation status, which modulates AJ stability and integrity of junctions.
source: VE-cadherin-catenin interactions are highly regulated by their phosphorylation status, which modulates AJ stability and integrity of junctions (Smith et al., 2020; Eliceiri et al., 1999; Orsenigo et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: TJs are ubiquitously distributed but their composition and localisation appear more heterogeneous in comparison to AJs.
source: TJs are also ubiquitously distributed but are in comparison relatively less well defined, and their composition and localisation appear more heterogeneous in comparison to AJs.
evidence: This is a general characterization based on established knowledge.

claim: Numerous transmembrane proteins are associated with TJs, including members of the claudin family, the tight junction-associated MARVEL proteins, such as Occludin, the junction-associated molecule (JAM) family, and endothelial-cell selective adhesion molecule (ESAM).
source: Numerous transmembrane proteins are associated with TJs, including members of the claudin family, the tight junction-associated MARVEL proteins, such as Occludin, the junction-associated molecule (JAM) family, and endothelial-cell selective adhesion molecule (ESAM) (Greene et al., 2019; Nasdala et al., 2002; Martìn-Padura et al., 1998; Raleigh et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: With few exceptions, TJ proteins are broadly expressed and not unique to vascular ECs.
source: With few exceptions, TJ proteins are broadly expressed and not unique to vascular ECs.
evidence: This is a general characterization based on established knowledge.

claim: TJ proteins exist in homophilic complexes between adjacent ECs, as well as with intracellular scaffolding proteins including members of the zonula occludens (ZO) family and Cingulin.
source: Similar to AJs, TJ proteins exist in homophilic complexes between adjacent ECs, as well as with intracellular scaffolding proteins including members of the zonula occludens (ZO) family and Cingulin (Stevenson et al., 1986; Schossleitner et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Claudin5 is highly expressed in the brain vasculature.
source: Claudin5 is highly expressed in the brain vasculature and is an important component of the blood brain barrier (BBB) and blood retinal barrier (BRB) where it is responsible for restricting the passage of small molecules (Daneman et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: Claudin5 is an important component of the blood brain barrier (BBB) and blood retinal barrier (BRB) where it is responsible for restricting the passage of small molecules.
source: Claudin5 is highly expressed in the brain vasculature and is an important component of the blood brain barrier (BBB) and blood retinal barrier (BRB) where it is responsible for restricting the passage of small molecules (Daneman et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: Constitutive Cldn5 knock-out in mice results in aberrant BBB permeability and death 10 hours after birth.
source: Consequently, constitutive Cldn5 knock-out in mice results in aberrant BBB permeability and death 10 hours after birth (Nitta et al., 2003).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: Downregulation of Claudin5 expression, and subsequent enhanced EC permeability, is associated with neurological disorders such as multiple sclerosis, stroke, epilepsy and schizophrenia.
source: Furthermore, downregulation of Claudin5 expression, and subsequent enhanced EC permeability, is associated with neurological disorders such as multiple sclerosis, stroke, epilepsy and schizophrenia (Alvarez et al., 2011; Knowland et al., 2014; Yan et al., 2018; Sun et al., 2004).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Outside of the CNS, Claudin5 is expressed in ECs to a lower degree, as are other TJ proteins such as Occludin.
source: Outside of the CNS, Claudin5 is expressed in ECs to a lower degree, as are other TJ proteins such as Occludin (Scalise et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: Non-CNS blood vessels have a more permeable EC barrier.
source: Consequently, non-CNS blood vessels have a more permeable EC barrier, although EC permeability also differs greatly between these peripheral tissues and is inherently linked to organ-specific function (Richards et al., 2021; Augustin and Koh, 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: EC permeability differs greatly between peripheral tissues and is inherently linked to organ-specific function.
source: Consequently, non-CNS blood vessels have a more permeable EC barrier, although EC permeability also differs greatly between these peripheral tissues and is inherently linked to organ-specific function (Richards et al., 2021; Augustin and Koh, 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: EC barrier integrity differs between vessel subtypes within vascular beds.
source: Furthermore, EC barrier integrity differs between vessel subtypes within these vascular beds (McDonald, 1994; Honkura et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The arteriolar aspect of the vasculature is more resistant to EC barrier disruption than the venular side.
source: Typically, the arteriolar aspect of the vasculature is more resistant to EC barrier disruption than the venular side.
evidence: This is established knowledge about vascular physiology.

claim: In the mouse ear dermis, EC barrier integrity correlates with Claudin5 expression, which is evident in arterioles but progressively diminishes in capillaries and venules.
source: Interestingly, at least in the mouse ear dermis, EC barrier integrity correlates with Claudin5 expression, which is evident in arterioles but progressively diminishes in capillaries and venules (Honkura et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: Assembly of multiple single-cell RNAseq datasets into a single integrated database revealed the variability and commonalities of EC barrier patterning.
source: Assembly of multiple single-cell RNAseq datasets into a single integrated database revealed the variability and commonalities of EC barrier patterning.
evidence: Supported by the scRNAseq analysis presented in Figure 1.

claim: In all tissues examined (ear skin, back skin, trachea, skeletal muscle and heart), Cldn5 exhibits decreasing expression along the arteriovenous axis.
source: In all tissues examined here; ear skin, back skin, trachea, skeletal muscle and heart, Cldn5 exhibits decreasing expression along the arteriovenous axis.
evidence: Supported by scRNAseq data shown in Figure 1.

claim: Cldn5 expression inversely correlates with histamine-induced vascular leakage.
source: We show that Cldn5 expression inversely correlates with histamine-induced vascular leakage, although precise patterning exhibits tissue-specific variability.
evidence: Supported by leakage assays shown in Figure 2.

claim: Precise patterning of Cldn5 expression exhibits tissue-specific variability.
source: We show that Cldn5 expression inversely correlates with histamine-induced vascular leakage, although precise patterning exhibits tissue-specific variability.
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 2.

claim: Systemic administration of tamoxifen to Cldn5 iECKO mice led to no obvious physiological or behavioral defects the first five days following treatment completion.
source: Systemic administration of tamoxifen to these 8–16 weeks old mice (Figure 3A) led to no obvious physiological or behavioral defects the first five days following treatment completion.
evidence: This is an observational finding from the experiments.

claim: Analysis of lung lysates showed a 60% reduction in Claudin5 protein levels in iECKO mice compared to controls.
source: Analysis of lung lysates showed a 60% reduction in Claudin5 protein levels and a near total loss of Cldn5 RNA in iECKO mice compared to controls (Figure 3B-D).
evidence: Supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 3B-C.

claim: Analysis of lung lysates showed a near total loss of Cldn5 RNA in iECKO mice compared to controls.
source: Analysis of lung lysates showed a 60% reduction in Claudin5 protein levels and a near total loss of Cldn5 RNA in iECKO mice compared to controls (Figure 3B-D).
evidence: Supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Blood vessels in the ear dermis showed an approximately 75% reduction in Claudin5 levels in iECKO mice, with some remaining protein expression evident in arterioles.
source: Blood vessels in the ear dermis meanwhile showed an approximately 75% reduction in Claudin5 levels, as discerned by immunofluorescent staining, with some remaining protein expression evident in arterioles (Figure 3E).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: The back skin showed relatively high basal permeability when compared with ear skin.
source: Interestingly, the back skin showed relatively high basal permeability when compared with ear skin, which showed minor dextran extravasation, while there was no basal leakage from skeletal muscle and heart.
evidence: Supported by permeability assay data shown in Figure 3F.

claim: Ear skin showed minor dextran extravasation at baseline.
source: Interestingly, the back skin showed relatively high basal permeability when compared with ear skin, which showed minor dextran extravasation, while there was no basal leakage from skeletal muscle and heart.
evidence: Supported by permeability assay data shown in Figure 3F.

claim: There was no basal leakage from skeletal muscle and heart.
source: Interestingly, the back skin showed relatively high basal permeability when compared with ear skin, which showed minor dextran extravasation, while there was no basal leakage from skeletal muscle and heart.
evidence: Supported by permeability assay data shown in Figure 3F.

claim: Basal permeability was unaffected by loss of Claudin5 when comparing Cldn5 iECKO with Cre-negative control mice, for all sizes of dextran investigated.
source: This basal permeability was unaffected by loss of Claudin5 when comparing Cldn5 iECKO with Cre-negative control mice, for all sizes of dextran investigated (Figure 3G).
evidence: Supported by permeability assay data shown in Figure 3G.

claim: In Cldn5 iECKO mice, the heart vasculature showed high resistance to histamine-mediated leakage, exhibiting an at least 100-fold lower dextran signal than other tissues.
source: In Cldn5 iECKO mice, the heart vasculature still showed high resistance to histamine-mediated leakage, exhibiting an at least 100-fold lower dextran signal than other tissues (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Supported by leakage assay data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The skeletal muscle vasculature showed no significant change in permeability upon loss of Cldn5.
source: The skeletal muscle vasculature also showed no significant change in permeability upon loss of Cldn5 (Figure 3H).
evidence: Supported by leakage assay data shown in Figure 3H.

claim: In the ear dermis, systemic administration of histamine resulted in a more than twofold increase in the extravasation of 2000 kDa dextran in Cldn5 iECKO mice.
source: In contrast, in the ear dermis, systemic administration of histamine resulted in a more than twofold increase in the extravasation of 2000 kDa dextran in Cldn5 iECKO mice (Figure 3I).
evidence: Supported by leakage assay data shown in Figure 3I.

claim: Both back skin and trachea vasculatures showed a significant 1.5-fold increase in the leakage of 2000 kDa dextran in Cldn5 iECKO mice compared to control.
source: Both back skin and trachea vasculatures showed a significant 1.5-fold increase in the leakage of 2000 kDa dextran in Cldn5 iECKO mice compared to control (Figure 3J and K).
evidence: Supported by leakage assay data shown in Figure 3J and K.

claim: Following onset of dermal inflammation, there was a significant increase in vascular leakage in the ear dermis of Cldn5 iECKO mice compared to control.
source: Following onset of dermal inflammation fluorescent tracers were administered and their subsequent extravasation analysed. This showed a significant increase in vascular leakage in the ear dermis (Figure 3L), but only a minor increase in the back skin, of Cldn5 iECKO mice compared to control (Figure 3M), in keeping with a more limited role for Claudin5 in the back skin versus the ear skin (Figure 3I and J).
evidence: Supported by Oxazolone-induced dermatitis data shown in Figure 3L.

claim: Following onset of dermal inflammation, there was only a minor increase in vascular leakage in the back skin of Cldn5 iECKO mice compared to control.
source: Following onset of dermal inflammation fluorescent tracers were administered and their subsequent extravasation analysed. This showed a significant increase in vascular leakage in the ear dermis (Figure 3L), but only a minor increase in the back skin, of Cldn5 iECKO mice compared to control (Figure 3M), in keeping with a more limited role for Claudin5 in the back skin versus the ear skin (Figure 3I and J).
evidence: Supported by Oxazolone-induced dermatitis data shown in Figure 3M.

claim: Claudin5 has a limited role in maintaining baseline EC barrier integrity in blood vessels outside of the CNS.
source: Claudin5 thus has a limited role in maintaining baseline EC barrier integrity in blood vessels outside of the CNS but is involved in the protection of vessels against agonist-induced macromolecular leakage in an organotypic manner.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the basal permeability data in Figure 3G.

claim: Claudin5 is involved in the protection of vessels against agonist-induced macromolecular leakage in an organotypic manner.
source: Claudin5 thus has a limited role in maintaining baseline EC barrier integrity in blood vessels outside of the CNS but is involved in the protection of vessels against agonist-induced macromolecular leakage in an organotypic manner.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the histamine-induced leakage data in Figures 3H-M.

claim: In the ear skin, expression of Claudin5 in arterioles was clearly reduced with some sporadic expression in Cldn5 iECKO mice.
source: In the ear skin, expression of Claudin5 in arterioles was clearly reduced with some sporadic expression in Cldn5 iECKO mice (Figure 4A).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Arterioles remained resistant to histamine-induced leakage even with reduced Claudin5 expression.
source: Even so, these vessels remained resistant to histamine-induced leakage.
evidence: Supported by leakage data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Topical 4-hydroxytamoxifen treatment increased loss of Claudin5 protein to approximately 85%.
source: Resultant loss of Claudin5 protein increased to approximately 85% (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Some remaining Claudin5 protein could be seen in arterioles and post-arteriolar capillaries after topical tamoxifen treatment.
source: The use of a Rosa26 lox-STOP-lox-YFP reporter revealed high levels of recombination, however some remaining Claudin5 protein could be seen in arterioles and post-arteriolar capillaries (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Topically tamoxifen treated mice showed a similar increase in histamine-induced 2000 kDa dextran leakage as systemically tamoxifen treated mice.
source: Furthermore, these mice showed a similar increase in histamine-induced 2000 kDa dextran leakage as systemically tamoxifen treated mice and arterial ECs were resistant to leakage, even when devoid of apparent Claudin5 expression (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Supported by leakage data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Arterial ECs were resistant to leakage, even when devoid of apparent Claudin5 expression.
source: Furthermore, these mice showed a similar increase in histamine-induced 2000 kDa dextran leakage as systemically tamoxifen treated mice and arterial ECs were resistant to leakage, even when devoid of apparent Claudin5 expression (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Supported by leakage data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Hrh1 and Hrh2 were generally either absent or expressed evenly between EC subtypes in all tissues.
source: However, Hrh1 and Hrh2, the main histamine receptors believed to be involved in EC barrier disruption (Adderley et al., 2015; Luo et al., 2013), were generally either absent or expressed evenly between EC subtypes in all tissues (Figure 4—figure supplement 1D, Figure 1—source data 1–4).
evidence: Supported by scRNAseq data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Hrh1 showed a slight increase in the venous populations in tracheal ECs.
source: Hrh1 and Hrh2 did however show a slight increase in the venous populations in tracheal and skeletal muscle ECs capillary populations of skeletal muscle, respectively.
evidence: Supported by scRNAseq data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Hrh2 showed a slight increase in capillary populations of skeletal muscle.
source: Hrh1 and Hrh2 did however show a slight increase in the venous populations in tracheal and skeletal muscle ECs capillary populations of skeletal muscle, respectively.
evidence: Supported by scRNAseq data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1D.

claim: More leakage sites were induced per vessel length after histamine stimulation in the Cldn5 iECKO ear dermis.
source: Intravital visualisation of vascular leakage following intradermal histamine administration confirmed the EC barrier protective properties of Claudin5, with more leakage sites being induced per vessel length after histamine stimulation in the Cldn5 iECKO ear dermis (Figure 4B and C and Video 2).
evidence: Supported by intravital imaging data shown in Figure 4B and C.

claim: The extent of barrier disruption at each site of leakage was increased, with individual leakage sites exhibiting enhanced extravasation of dextran following Claudin5 loss.
source: The extent of barrier disruption at each site of leakage was also increased, with individual leakage sites exhibiting enhanced extravasation of dextran following Claudin5 loss (Figure 4D).
evidence: Supported by intravital imaging data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: The time lag of endothelial response to stimulation was unchanged, with leakage occurring approximately 3 min after stimulation in Cldn5 iECKO mice and their controls.
source: The time lag of endothelial response to stimulation was however unchanged, with leakage occurring approximately 3 min after stimulation in Cldn5 iECKO mice and their controls (Figure 4E).
evidence: Supported by intravital imaging data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: Small vessels (5–10 µm) and subsequent mid-sized venules (10–15 µm) leaked to a greater degree following the loss of Claudin5.
source: This analysis showed that small vessels (5–10 µm) and subsequent mid-sized venules (10–15 µm) leaked to a greater degree following the loss of Claudin5.
evidence: Supported by vessel diameter analysis shown in Figure 4F.

claim: Larger venules (15–20 μm) showed no change in leakage following the loss of Claudin5.
source: In contrast, larger venules (15–20 μm) showed no change in leakage (Figure 4F).
evidence: Supported by vessel diameter analysis shown in Figure 4F.

claim: In the ear skin of Cldn5(BAC)-GFP mice, arteriolar αSMA coverage ends before Cldn5(BAC)-GFP expression.
source: In the ear skin of Cldn5(BAC)-GFP mice, arteriolar αSMA coverage can be seen to end before Cldn5(BAC)-GFP expression, whilst its venular expression begins after Cldn5(BAC)-GFP expression has been lost (Figure 4—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1E.

claim: Venular αSMA expression begins after Cldn5(BAC)-GFP expression has been lost.
source: In the ear skin of Cldn5(BAC)-GFP mice, arteriolar αSMA coverage can be seen to end before Cldn5(BAC)-GFP expression, whilst its venular expression begins after Cldn5(BAC)-GFP expression has been lost (Figure 4—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1E.

claim: Cldn5(BAC)-GFP expression is lost in the αSMA-negative capillary bed.
source: Cldn5(BAC)-GFP expression is thus lost in the αSMA-negative capillary bed.
evidence: This is an inference from the αSMA and Cldn5(BAC)-GFP expression patterns.

claim: There was an almost total loss of Claudin5 levels in capillaries and a 75% reduction in αSMA-positive arterioles in Cldn5 iECKO mice.
source: Based on this segregation we observed an almost total loss of Claudin5 levels in capillaries and a 75% reduction in αSMA-positive arterioles (Figure 4—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1F.

claim: Following histamine stimulation, there was a 2.5-fold increase in leakage from αSMA-positive venules in Cldn5 iECKO mice.
source: Following histamine stimulation, analysis showed a 2.5-fold increase in leakage from αSMA-positive venules and a fourfold increase in leakage in αSMA-negative capillaries in Cldn5 iECKO mice (Figure 4G and H).
evidence: Supported by leakage analysis shown in Figure 4H.

claim: Following histamine stimulation, there was a fourfold increase in leakage in αSMA-negative capillaries in Cldn5 iECKO mice.
source: Following histamine stimulation, analysis showed a 2.5-fold increase in leakage from αSMA-positive venules and a fourfold increase in leakage in αSMA-negative capillaries in Cldn5 iECKO mice (Figure 4G and H).
evidence: Supported by leakage analysis shown in Figure 4H.

claim: In Cldn5 iECKO mice, leakage sites appeared closer to arterioles than in controls.
source: Furthermore, in Cldn5 iECKO mice, leakage sites appeared closer to arterioles than in controls (Figure 4I).
evidence: Supported by distance analysis shown in Figure 4I.

claim: Any dextran signal associated with arterioles was negligible and unaffected by the loss of Claudin5.
source: As expected, any dextran signal associated with arterioles was negligible and unaffected by the loss of Claudin5.
evidence: Supported by leakage analysis shown in Figure 4H.

claim: In Cldn5(BAC)-GFP-negative vessels, Cldn5 expression still occurred, albeit to a considerably lower level than Cldn5(BAC)-GFP-positive vessels.
source: Use of more sensitive RNA in situ hybridisation, however, showed that in Cldn5(BAC)-GFP-negative vessels Cldn5 expression still occurred, albeit to a considerably lower level than Cldn5(BAC)-GFP-positive vessels, in keeping with the expression patterning observed from scRNAseq data (Figure 1F and Figure 4J).
evidence: Supported by RNA in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 4J.

claim: In the wild-type vasculature, Claudin5 is responsible for limiting the disruption of EC junctions in capillaries, but also in immediately following venules.
source: From the highly sensitive RNA in situ detection of Cldn5 expression in capillaries and postcapillary venules, we conclude that in the wild-type vasculature, Claudin5 is responsible for limiting the disruption of EC junctions in capillaries, but also in immediately following venules.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the RNA in situ and leakage data.

claim: Arterioles remain resistant to agonist-induced leakage, presumably due to residual Claudin5 expression and the relatively high expression of other TJ components.
source: Arterioles remain resistant to agonist-induced leakage, as do larger venules, presumably due to residual Claudin5 expression and the relatively high expression of other TJ components.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the observed resistance of arterioles to leakage.

claim: There was no obvious change in junction structure after loss of Claudin5 as assessed by TEM.
source: Analysis of the electron dense area, width and density showed that there was no obvious change in this junction structure after loss of Claudin5 (Figure 5A–C).
evidence: Supported by TEM analysis shown in Figure 5A-C.

claim: Greater disruption of the endothelial barrier was seen following histamine stimulation in Cldn5 iECKO mice, allowing greater penetrance of horse radish peroxidase (HRP) into the intercellular cleft.
source: In keeping with the enhanced leakage that we observed following the loss of Claudin5, greater disruption of the endothelial barrier was seen following histamine stimulation, allowing greater penetrance of horse radish peroxidase (HRP) into the intercellular cleft (Figure 5D).
evidence: Supported by TEM analysis with HRP shown in Figure 5D.

claim: Following Cldn5 KO, small increases in Cdh5, Ocln and F11r expression were observed in lung RNA.
source: Following Cldn5 KO, small increases in Cdh5, Ocln and F11r expression, but a decrease in Tjp1 expression was observed (Figure 5E).
evidence: Supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 5E.

claim: Following Cldn5 KO, a decrease in Tjp1 expression was observed in lung RNA.
source: Following Cldn5 KO, small increases in Cdh5, Ocln and F11r expression, but a decrease in Tjp1 expression was observed (Figure 5E).
evidence: Supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 5E.

claim: Analysis of lung protein samples confirmed the enhanced protein expression of VE-Cadherin and Occludin and decrease in ZO-1.
source: Subsequent analysis of lung protein samples confirmed the enhanced protein expression of VE-Cadherin and Occludin and decrease in ZO-1 (Figure 5F, Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 5F.

claim: Claudin5 expression levels inversely correlate with VE-Cadherin and Occludin.
source: Correlation analysis of these samples also supported this finding, with Claudin5 expression levels inversely correlating with VE-Cadherin and Occludin and positively correlating with ZO-1, but not JAM-A, Cingulin, or ESAM (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Claudin5 expression levels positively correlate with ZO-1.
source: Correlation analysis of these samples also supported this finding, with Claudin5 expression levels inversely correlating with VE-Cadherin and Occludin and positively correlating with ZO-1, but not JAM-A, Cingulin, or ESAM (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Claudin5 expression levels do not correlate with JAM-A, Cingulin, or ESAM.
source: Correlation analysis of these samples also supported this finding, with Claudin5 expression levels inversely correlating with VE-Cadherin and Occludin and positively correlating with ZO-1, but not JAM-A, Cingulin, or ESAM (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Immunohistochemistry analysis of the ear dermis showed a downregulation of ZO-1 in Cldn5 iECKO mice.
source: Immunohistochemistry analysis of the ear dermis similarly showed a downregulation of ZO-1 and an upregulation of VE-Cadherin in Cldn5 iECKO mice (Figure 5G and H).
evidence: Supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 5G.

claim: Immunohistochemistry analysis of the ear dermis showed an upregulation of VE-Cadherin in Cldn5 iECKO mice.
source: Immunohistochemistry analysis of the ear dermis similarly showed a downregulation of ZO-1 and an upregulation of VE-Cadherin in Cldn5 iECKO mice (Figure 5G and H).
evidence: Supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 5H.

claim: ZO-1 and VE-Cadherin levels were unchanged in ECs of the back skin of Cldn5 iECKO compared to control.
source: In contrast, ZO-1 and VE-Cadherin levels were unchanged in ECs of the back skin of Cldn5 iECKO compared to control (Figure 5I).
evidence: Supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 5I.

claim: ZO-1 expression was significantly decreased specifically in venules in the ear skin.
source: ZO-1 expression was found to be significantly decreased specifically in venules whilst VE-Cadherin was equally upregulated in both capillaries and venules, but not in arterioles (Figure 5J and K).
evidence: Supported by vessel subtype analysis shown in Figure 5J.

claim: VE-Cadherin was equally upregulated in both capillaries and venules, but not in arterioles in the ear skin.
source: ZO-1 expression was found to be significantly decreased specifically in venules whilst VE-Cadherin was equally upregulated in both capillaries and venules, but not in arterioles (Figure 5J and K).
evidence: Supported by vessel subtype analysis shown in Figure 5K.

claim: Claudin5 expression regulates the expression and localisation of other EC junction components.
source: Claudin5 expression thus regulates the expression and localisation of other EC junction components.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the junction protein expression data in Figure 5.

claim: Whilst Claudin5 loss results in no overt changes in junction structure, in a tissue-specific manner it alters the regulatable and dynamic nature of the remaining junctional complex leading to changes in barrier stability.
source: Consequently, whilst Claudin5 loss results in no overt changes in junction structure, in a tissue-specific manner it alters the regulatable and dynamic nature of the remaining junctional complex leading to changes in barrier stability.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the TEM and junction protein expression data.

claim: Vessels in the ear skin, back skin, trachea, skeletal muscle, and the heart share a similar complement of AJ and TJ genes.
source: Broadly, vessels in the ear skin, back skin, trachea, skeletal muscle, and the heart share a similar complement of AJ and TJ genes.
evidence: Supported by scRNAseq analysis shown in Figure 1.

claim: Subtle variation in the relative distribution of AJ and TJ genes between different vessel subsets are often evident.
source: Still, subtle variation in their relative distribution between different vessel subsets are often evident, as is variability in EC barrier integrity and response to stimulation in diverse tissues.
evidence: Supported by scRNAseq analysis shown in Figure 1.

claim: There is variability in EC barrier integrity and response to stimulation in diverse tissues.
source: Still, subtle variation in their relative distribution between different vessel subsets are often evident, as is variability in EC barrier integrity and response to stimulation in diverse tissues.
evidence: Supported by leakage assays shown in Figure 2.

claim: Transmembrane TJ genes were found to be expressed to a greater degree in the arterial aspect of the microvasculature.
source: Generally, transmembrane TJ genes were found to be expressed to a greater degree in the arterial aspect of the microvasculature.
evidence: Supported by scRNAseq analysis shown in Figure 1.

claim: Cldn5 exhibited a large gradual decrease in expression from arterioles through capillaries to venules in all tissues analysed, including in the human dermis.
source: In particular, Cldn5 stands out in this analysis as it exhibited a large gradual decrease in expression from arterioles through capillaries to venules in all tissues analysed, including in the human dermis.
evidence: Supported by scRNAseq analysis shown in Figure 1.

claim: In the ear skin, Claudin5 expression inversely correlates with susceptibility to VEGF-A-induced leakage, with capillaries possessing a mixture of Claudin5-positive and -negative cells being responsive to leakage stimulation.
source: Previously we have shown that, in the ear skin, Claudin5 expression inversely correlates with susceptibility to VEGF-A-induced leakage, with capillaries possessing a mixture of Claudin5-positive and -negative cells being responsive to leakage stimulation (Honkura et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior work.

claim: The correlation between Claudin5 expression and leakage susceptibility does not extend to other vascular beds such as the back skin and trachea, in which the leakage permissive vasculature was shifted away from the capillary region toward the venous side.
source: This correlation however does not extend to other vascular beds such as the back skin and trachea, in which the leakage permissive vasculature was shifted away from the capillary region toward the venous side.
evidence: Supported by leakage analysis shown in Figure 2.

claim: The trachea shows a much larger leakage response overall than the ear skin.
source: Of note, whilst tracheal capillaries might be resistant to leakage, the trachea shows a much larger leakage response overall than the ear skin.
evidence: Supported by leakage analysis shown in Figure 2H.

claim: The back skin showed a larger leakage response than the ear skin.
source: The back skin similarly showed a larger leakage response than the ear skin.
evidence: Supported by leakage analysis shown in Figure 2H.

claim: Outside of the CNS, the largest influence of Claudin5 is in the ear skin among the organs analysed.
source: We find that outside of the CNS, the largest influence of Claudin5 is in the ear skin among the organs analysed, with a more modest loss in barrier integrity also observed in back skin and tracheal vasculatures.
evidence: Supported by leakage analysis in Cldn5 iECKO mice shown in Figure 3.

claim: A more modest loss in barrier integrity was observed in back skin and tracheal vasculatures following Claudin5 loss.
source: We find that outside of the CNS, the largest influence of Claudin5 is in the ear skin among the organs analysed, with a more modest loss in barrier integrity also observed in back skin and tracheal vasculatures.
evidence: Supported by leakage analysis in Cldn5 iECKO mice shown in Figure 3.

claim: EC barrier integrity in skeletal muscle and heart showed no change following the loss of Claudin5.
source: EC barrier integrity in skeletal muscle and heart meanwhile showed no change following the loss of Claudin5.
evidence: Supported by leakage analysis in Cldn5 iECKO mice shown in Figure 3H and Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The differential effect of Claudin5 loss might be explained by the expression patterning of Cldn5, which declines more proximal to the arterial side along the arteriovenous axis in skeletal muscle than tissue such as the ear skin.
source: This observation might be explained by the expression patterning of Cldn5, which declines more proximal to the arterial side along the arteriovenous axis in skeletal muscle than tissue such as the ear skin (Figure 1F).
evidence: This is a speculative explanation based on expression data.

claim: Expression of other TJ genes, such as Ocln, Nectin2 and Nectin3, is observed in skeletal muscle and heart which are not evident in the other tissues analysed.
source: Alternatively, we observe expression of other TJ genes, such as Ocln, Nectin2 and Nectin3, in skeletal muscle and heart which are not evident in the other tissues analysed.
evidence: Supported by scRNAseq analysis shown in Figure 1.

claim: Other studies have demonstrated a barrier protective role for Occludin, nectin-2 and nectin-3 in vitro.
source: Other studies have demonstrated a barrier protective role for Occludin, nectin-2 and nectin-3 in vitro (Martin et al., 2013; Son et al., 2016; Murakami et al., 2009), but further studies are required to establish whether these actively participate in EC barrier integrity in vivo (Saitou et al., 2000).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Loss of Claudin5 did not alter BEC junction structure in the ear dermis.
source: In keeping with previous observations in the brain, loss of Claudin5 did not alter BEC junction structure in the ear dermis (Nitta et al., 2003).
evidence: Supported by TEM analysis shown in Figure 5A-C and citation to prior literature.

claim: Loss of VE-Cadherin in the lungs enhances barrier permeability without causing any structural defects.
source: Similarly, loss of VE-Cadherin in the lungs enhances barrier permeability without causing any structural defects (Duong et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: Concomitant loss of ESAM along with VE-Cadherin produces more overt changes in junction structure and enhances loss of barrier integrity.
source: Interestingly, concomitant loss of ESAM along with VE-Cadherin produces more overt changes in junction structure and enhances loss of barrier integrity, highlighting the redundant organisation of the EC barrier (Duong et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: Assembly of VE-Cadherin junctions upregulates Claudin5 expression.
source: Assembly of VE-Cadherin junctions upregulates Claudin5 expression, whilst its loss leads to compensatory upregulation of N-Cadherin (Taddei et al., 2008; Giampietro et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Loss of VE-Cadherin leads to compensatory upregulation of N-Cadherin.
source: Assembly of VE-Cadherin junctions upregulates Claudin5 expression, whilst its loss leads to compensatory upregulation of N-Cadherin (Taddei et al., 2008; Giampietro et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Claudin5 can reciprocally alter expression of VE-Cadherin, as well as Occludin and ZO-1 in vivo.
source: We find here in vivo that Claudin5 can reciprocally alter expression of VE-Cadherin, as well as Occludin and ZO-1 (Figure 5E and F).
evidence: Supported by qPCR and Western blot data shown in Figure 5E and F.

claim: Tight junctions have been suggested to control gene expression through ZO-1's tension-dependent interaction with the ZO-1–associated nucleic acid binding protein (ZONAB).
source: Tight junctions have previously been suggested to control gene expression through ZO-1's tension-dependent interaction with the ZO-1–associated nucleic acid binding protein (ZONAB) (Balda and Matter, 2000; Spadaro et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: When under tension ZO-1 can interact with ZONAB, resulting its junctional sequestering.
source: When under tension ZO-1 can interact with ZONAB, resulting its junctional sequestering.
evidence: This is established knowledge about ZO-1 function.

claim: ZO-1 interacts with Claudins through their PDZ domains.
source: ZO-1 also interacts with Claudins through their PDZ domains (Itoh et al., 1999).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: Loss of junctional Claudin5 and resulting dislocation of junctional ZONAB may modify the EC transcriptome.
source: Loss of junctional Claudin5 and resulting dislocation of junctional ZONAB may thus modify the EC transcriptome.
evidence: This is a speculative mechanism to explain the observed changes in gene expression.

claim: Upregulation of VE-Cadherin may explain the lack of structural defects of junctions in Cldn5 iECKO mice.
source: Upregulation of VE-Cadherin meanwhile may explain the lack of structural defects of junctions in Cldn5 iECKO mice.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the TEM findings.

claim: VE-Cadherin at junctions is highly dynamic and its localisation is regulated by numerous cytokines and growth factors that affect its phosphorylation status.
source: Moreover, in contrast to Claudin5, VE-Cadherin at junctions is highly dynamic and its localisation is regulated by numerous cytokines and growth factors that affect its phosphorylation status (Smith et al., 2020; Orsenigo et al., 2012; Eliceiri et al., 1999).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Upregulation of VE-Cadherin by Claudin5 deficiency is likely to produce junctions that are less stable and subject to higher turnover in a stimulatory environment.
source: Upregulation of VE-Cadherin by Claudin5 deficiency is therefore likely to produce junctions that are less stable and subject to higher turnover in a stimulatory environment.
evidence: This is a speculative conclusion based on VE-Cadherin properties.

claim: Pericytes are known to be essential for maintenance of the tight BBB.
source: Pericytes are known to be essential for maintenance of the tight BBB (Armulik et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: Outside of the CNS pericyte coverage is comparatively low.
source: Outside of the CNS however pericyte coverage is comparatively low and whether coverage differs between non-CNS vascular beds is unknown.
evidence: This is established knowledge about pericyte distribution.

claim: Barrier integrity may be regulated by basement membrane components such as laminin α5, which enhances VE-Cadherin stability at cell-cell junctions.
source: Barrier integrity may also be regulated by basement membrane components such as laminin α5, which enhances VE-Cadherin stability at cell-cell junctions (Richards et al., 2021; Song et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Basement membrane coverage differs between different vascular beds, as well as between vessel subtypes.
source: Similar to pericytes, basement membrane coverage differs between different vascular beds, as well as between vessel subtypes (Richards et al., 2021; Di Russo et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: In accordance with its role in forming the tight BBB and BRB in the CNS, Claudin5 influences vascular permeability in peripheral vascular beds, albeit in an organotypic and vessel-type manner.
source: In conclusion, this study provides an in-depth characterisation and comparison of the EC barrier in numerous organs. Furthermore, in accordance with its role in forming the tight BBB and BRB in the CNS, we find that Claudin5 influences vascular permeability in peripheral vascular beds, albeit in an organotypic and vessel-type manner.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion of the study findings.

claim: The impact of Claudin5 in organ-specific vascular permeability was demonstrated by the direct correlation between its expression and high barrier integrity in some, but not all vascular beds.
source: The impact of Claudin5 in organ-specific vascular permeability was demonstrated by the direct correlation between its expression and high barrier integrity in some, but not all vascular beds.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion of the study findings.

claim: Cdh5 (VE-Cadherin) was ubiquitously expressed within each organ but was generally slightly lower in venous vessels compared to other subsets within these tissues.
source: The adherens junction gene Cdh5 (VE-Cadherin) was ubiquitously expressed within each organ but was generally slightly lower in venous vessels compared to other subsets within these tissues (Figure 1E).
evidence: Supported by scRNAseq data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: N-Cadherin (Cdh2) expression was relatively low in all organs.
source: Moreover, N-Cadherin (Cdh2) expression was relatively low, whereas T-Cadherin (Cdh13) was high, in all organs (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Supported by scRNAseq data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: T-Cadherin (Cdh13) was highly expressed in all organs.
source: Moreover, N-Cadherin (Cdh2) expression was relatively low, whereas T-Cadherin (Cdh13) was high, in all organs (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Supported by scRNAseq data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: The cell adhesion molecule Caecam1 was relatively abundantly expressed in all organs.
source: The cell adhesion molecule Caecam1 was also relatively abundantly expressed in all organs.
evidence: Supported by scRNAseq data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: The Nectins 1, 2 and 3 showed expression restricted to skeletal and heart muscle ECs.
source: Meanwhile, the Nectins 1, 2 and 3 showed expression restricted to skeletal and heart muscle ECs.
evidence: Supported by scRNAseq data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: Intracellular junction proteins such as α-, β- and p120-catenin (Ctnna1, Ctnnb1, Ctnnd1, respectively) were ubiquitously expressed.
source: As expected, intracellular junction proteins such as α-, β- and p120-catenin (Ctnna1, Ctnnb1, Ctnnd1, respectively) were ubiquitously expressed, as were ZO-1 (Tjp1) and ZO-2 (Tjp2) and the angiomotin-like proteins 1 and 2 (Amotl1 and Amotl2) (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Supported by scRNAseq data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: ZO-1 (Tjp1) and ZO-2 (Tjp2) were ubiquitously expressed.
source: As expected, intracellular junction proteins such as α-, β- and p120-catenin (Ctnna1, Ctnnb1, Ctnnd1, respectively) were ubiquitously expressed, as were ZO-1 (Tjp1) and ZO-2 (Tjp2) and the angiomotin-like proteins 1 and 2 (Amotl1 and Amotl2) (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Supported by scRNAseq data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: The angiomotin-like proteins 1 and 2 (Amotl1 and Amotl2) were ubiquitously expressed.
source: As expected, intracellular junction proteins such as α-, β- and p120-catenin (Ctnna1, Ctnnb1, Ctnnd1, respectively) were ubiquitously expressed, as were ZO-1 (Tjp1) and ZO-2 (Tjp2) and the angiomotin-like proteins 1 and 2 (Amotl1 and Amotl2) (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Supported by scRNAseq data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: The JAM family of junctional adhesion molecules (F11r, Jam2, Jam3) exhibited reasonably homogenous expression, but was occasionally more abundantly expressed in capillaries than in arteries and veins, in an organotypic manner.
source: The JAM family of junctional adhesion molecules (F11r, Jam2, Jam3) exhibited reasonably homogenous expression, but was occasionally more abundantly expressed in capillaries than in arteries and veins, in an organotypic manner (Figure 1E, Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Supported by scRNAseq data shown in Figure 1E and Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: Esam was homogenously expressed with reduced expression in the venous subset of some tissues.
source: Esam similarly was homogenously expressed with reduced expression in the venous subset of some tissues (Figure 1E).
evidence: Supported by scRNAseq data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Expression of the tight junction-associated Marvel proteins (TAMPs) Ocln, Marveld2, and Marveld3 was relatively low, being limited to only a few BECs in an organotypic and subset-specific manner.
source: Expression of the tight junction-associated Marvel proteins (TAMPs) Ocln, Marveld2, and Marveld3 was relatively low, being limited to only a few BECs in an organotypic and subset-specific manner (Figure 1E, Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Supported by scRNAseq data shown in Figure 1E and Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: Most members of the Claudin family were expressed at a very low level with the exception of Cldn5, Cldn15, and Cldnd1.
source: Most members of the Claudin family were expressed at a very low level with the exception of Cldn5, Cldn15, and Cldnd1, the latter of which was specifically absent in the tracheal vasculature.
evidence: Supported by scRNAseq data shown in Figure 1E and Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: Cldnd1 was specifically absent in the tracheal vasculature.
source: Most members of the Claudin family were expressed at a very low level with the exception of Cldn5, Cldn15, and Cldnd1, the latter of which was specifically absent in the tracheal vasculature.
evidence: Supported by scRNAseq data shown in Figure 1E and Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: Both Cldn5 and Cldn15 exhibited diminishing expression along the arteriovenous axis.
source: Both Cldn5 and Cldn15, however, exhibited diminishing expression along the arteriovenous axis, with Cldn5 in particular exhibiting higher expression in arteries compared to veins, displaying fold changes between 3 (ear skin) and 15 (skeletal muscle) (Figure 1E and F).
evidence: Supported by scRNAseq data shown in Figure 1E and F.

claim: Cldn5 exhibited higher expression in arteries compared to veins, displaying fold changes between 3 (ear skin) and 15 (skeletal muscle).
source: Both Cldn5 and Cldn15, however, exhibited diminishing expression along the arteriovenous axis, with Cldn5 in particular exhibiting higher expression in arteries compared to veins, displaying fold changes between 3 (ear skin) and 15 (skeletal muscle) (Figure 1E and F).
evidence: Supported by scRNAseq data shown in Figure 1E and F.

claim: Analysis of genes differentially expressed between vessel subsets showed consistently significant changes in Cldn5 expression.
source: Accordingly, analysis of genes differentially expressed between vessel subsets showed consistently significant changes in Cldn5 expression (Figure 1—source data 1–4).
evidence: Supported by differential gene expression analysis.

claim: Human skin BECs showed enrichment of adherens junction genes CDH5 and CDH13 in the arterial and capillary subsets, with lower levels in venous proximal capillaries and veins.
source: Similar analysis of human skin BECs as employed for mouse BECs (Figure 1—figure supplement 4) showed enrichment of adherens junction genes CDH5 and CDH13 in the arterial and capillary subsets, with lower levels in venous proximal capillaries and veins (Figure 1—figure supplement 5).
evidence: Supported by scRNAseq data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 5.

claim: In human vasculature, F11R, ESAM, CLDN5, and CLDN10 expression was significantly higher in arteries and downregulated in veins.
source: In keeping with the overall trend in the mouse vasculature, human tight junction component expression was also relatively higher in arteries and/or capillaries; F11R, ESAM, CLDN5, and CLDN10 expression was significantly higher in arteries and downregulated in veins (Figure 1G, Figure 1—figure supplement 5, Figure 1—source data 5).
evidence: Supported by scRNAseq data shown in Figure 1G and Figure 1—figure supplement 5.

claim: In the ear dermis, expression of Claudin5 inversely correlates with vessel susceptibility to Vascular Endothelial Growth Factor A (VEGF-A)-induced leakage.
source: In the ear dermis, expression of Claudin5 inversely correlates with vessel susceptibility to Vascular Endothelial Growth Factor A (VEGF-A)-induced leakage (Honkura et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: Intradermal administration of histamine elicited a similar leakage patterning as previously shown for VEGF-A, with leakage occurring only in vessels possessing ECs lacking apparent Cldn5(BAC)-GFP expression.
source: Here, intradermal administration of histamine elicited a similar leakage patterning as previously shown for VEGF-A, with leakage occurring only in vessels possessing ECs lacking apparent Cldn5(BAC)-GFP expression (Figure 2A and B and Video 1).
evidence: Supported by intravital imaging data shown in Figure 2A and B.

claim: Within the leakage-susceptible vasculature, a population of Cldn5(BAC)-GFP-negative vessels failed to respond to histamine stimulation.
source: Interestingly, within the leakage-susceptible vasculature, a population of Cldn5(BAC)-GFP-negative vessels failed to respond to histamine stimulation, highlighting the potential importance of factors other than Claudin5 that influence vessel susceptibility to stimulation (Figure 2C; Richards et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by intravital imaging data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: When given systemically, histamine caused leakage in the ear dermis from venules and also from capillaries exhibiting a mixed expression of Cldn5(BAC)-GFP.
source: When given systemically, along with a 2000 kDa lysine-fixable dextran, histamine caused leakage in the ear dermis from venules and also from capillaries exhibiting a mixed expression of Cldn5(BAC)-GFP (Figure 2D, left).
evidence: Supported by systemic leakage assay data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Skeletal muscle showed leakage susceptibility starting in the capillary bed where Cldn5(BAC)-GFP expression was heterogeneous.
source: Skeletal muscle also showed leakage susceptibility starting in the capillary bed where Cldn5(BAC)-GFP expression was heterogeneous (Figure 2—figure supplement 1, left).
evidence: Supported by systemic leakage assay data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: The heart vasculature showed no extravascular dextran accumulation with or without histamine stimulation.
source: The heart vasculature meanwhile showed no extravascular dextran accumulation with or without histamine stimulation (Figure 2—figure supplement 1, right).
evidence: Supported by systemic leakage assay data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: The tracheal vasculature displayed a clear separation between Cldn5(BAC)-GFP-positive arterioles and leakage susceptible vessels, with the capillaries that cross the cartilage rings being Cldn5(BAC)-GFP-negative and resistant to stimulation.
source: Unlike the ear dermis and skeletal muscle, the tracheal vasculature displayed a clear separation between Cldn5(BAC)-GFP-positive arterioles and leakage susceptible vessels, with the capillaries that cross the cartilage rings being Cldn5(BAC)-GFP-negative and resistant to stimulation (Figure 2E, left).
evidence: Supported by systemic leakage assay data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: The mouse back skin revealed an intermediary phenotype, with vessels possessing a mixed expression of Cldn5(BAC)-GFP being largely resistant to leakage, whilst immediately subsequent venules exhibited a strong leakage phenotype.
source: Interestingly, examination of the mouse back skin revealed an intermediary phenotype, with vessels possessing a mixed expression of Cldn5(BAC)-GFP being largely resistant to leakage, whilst immediately subsequent venules exhibited a strong leakage phenotype (Figure 2F, left).
evidence: Supported by systemic leakage assay data shown in Figure 2F.

claim: The ear skin showed an increased proportion of extravasated dextran from Cldn5(BAC)-GFP-positive versus Cldn5(BAC)-GFP-negative vessels compared to back skin and trachea.
source: These differing leakage patterns were also apparent from the increased proportion of extravasated dextran from Cldn5(BAC)-GFP-positive versus Cldn5(BAC)-GFP-negative vessels in the ear skin compared to back skin and trachea (Figure 2G).
evidence: Supported by leakage quantification shown in Figure 2G.

claim: In response to the same histamine stimulus, leakage permissive vessels in the trachea and the back skin showed more extensive leakage as compared to the ear skin.
source: In response to the same stimulus, leakage permissive vessels in the trachea and the back skin showed more extensive leakage as compared to the ear skin.
evidence: Supported by leakage quantification shown in Figure 2H.

claim: Skeletal muscle showed a similar leakage response as the ear skin.
source: Skeletal muscle showed a similar leakage response as the ear skin whilst, as expected, no histamine-induced leakage was observed in the heart (Figure 2I).
evidence: Supported by leakage quantification shown in Figure 2I.

claim: No histamine-induced leakage was observed in the heart.
source: Skeletal muscle showed a similar leakage response as the ear skin whilst, as expected, no histamine-induced leakage was observed in the heart (Figure 2I).
evidence: Supported by leakage quantification shown in Figure 2I.

claim: Outside of the CNS, a zonation of Claudin5 expression exists along the arteriovenous axis.
source: This data shows that outside of the CNS, a zonation of Claudin5 expression exists along the arteriovenous axis.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the expression and leakage data.

claim: The relationship between Claudin5 expression and susceptibility to vascular leakage differs between vascular beds, particularly in capillaries.
source: Moreover, the relationship between Claudin5 expression and susceptibility to vascular leakage differs between vascular beds, particularly in capillaries, as does the sensitivity of ECs to stimulation and their resulting junctional disruption.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the leakage data in different tissues.

claim: The sensitivity of ECs to stimulation and their resulting junctional disruption differs between vascular beds.
source: Moreover, the relationship between Claudin5 expression and susceptibility to vascular leakage differs between vascular beds, particularly in capillaries, as does the sensitivity of ECs to stimulation and their resulting junctional disruption.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the leakage data in different tissues.
